slides.title: Global fisheries: scale, status, and stakes
slides.body:
**Capture fisheries**: ~80 million tonnes globally; ~$160B/yr industry; ~60M people employed (FAO SOFIA reports). Plus ~120 million tonnes from aquaculture (now > capture by tonnage since 2014). Together = ~17% of animal-protein consumption globally; >50% in coastal developing nations.

**Stock status** (FAO 2024):
- **Within biologically sustainable levels**: ~62% of assessed stocks (down from 90% in 1974).
- **Overfished** (below MSY-supporting biomass): ~38%.
- Specific examples: Atlantic cod, Atlantic bluefin tuna, Pacific bluefin tuna, many sharks, orange roughy, several skates + rays.

**Top fisheries by tonnage**:
- Peruvian anchoveta (Engraulis ringens): ~5-10M t/yr; fishmeal + oil.
- Alaska pollock (Theragra chalcogramma): ~3M t/yr; surimi.
- Skipjack tuna (Katsuwonus pelamis): ~3M t/yr; canned.
- Atlantic herring, capelin, mackerel.
- Japanese anchovy, sardine.
- Chub mackerel, blue whiting, gulf menhaden.

**Bycatch**: ~10% of catch is discarded — many species threatened (turtles, sharks, seabirds, marine mammals). Driftnet ban (UN 1991); ongoing efforts on longlines + trawls.

**IUU fishing** (illegal, unreported, unregulated): ~20% of catch in some regions; major issue in west Africa + SE Asia + high seas. Global Fishing Watch + AIS / VMS / satellite monitoring.

**The 'tragedy of the commons' problem**: open-access fisheries → fleet enters until profit = 0 → stock crashes. Modern solutions: catch shares (ITQs), territorial use rights (TURFs), MPAs, community management, certification (MSC).

slides.title: Stock assessment: VPA + integrated models
slides.body:
**Stock assessment**: estimate current biomass + fishing mortality + project future trajectories under different management.

**Single-species production models**:
- **Schaefer (1957)**: logistic with harvest. Estimates r, K, MSY. Simple but oversimplifies.
- **Fox**: Gompertz growth (different curvature).
- **Pella-Tomlinson**: generalized; flexibility in shape.

**Age-structured models** (current state of art):
- **Virtual population analysis (VPA / cohort analysis)**: back-calculate population at age in past years from catch-at-age. Pope's approximation.
- **Statistical catch-at-age (SCAA)**: integrated likelihood; estimate selectivity, mortality, recruitment.
- **Integrated Bayesian (Stock Synthesis, SS3)**: combine catch + survey + age + length + tagging data.

**Reference points**:
- **B_MSY**: biomass that gives MSY.
- **F_MSY**: fishing mortality that gives MSY.
- **B_lim / B_pa**: limit + precautionary biomass.
- **F_lim / F_pa**: limit + precautionary fishing mortality.
- Modern harvest control rules (HCRs): F as function of B (reduce F when B drops).

**Surveys** (independent of fishery):
- Bottom-trawl (NMFS surveys); acoustic (echo sounders for pelagics); ichthyoplankton; aerial; tag-recapture.
- Tagging: traditional + electronic (PSAT, acoustic, archival).
- eDNA + camera-based emerging.

**Uncertainty + management strategy evaluation (MSE)**: simulate stock + fishery + management under different scenarios; test robustness of harvest control rules. Closed-loop simulation. Now standard at ICES + RFMOs.

**Data-poor methods**: when catch is all you have, length-based methods (LBSPR, LIME), DCAC, depletion-corrected average catch.

**RAM Legacy Stock Assessment Database**: publicly available time series for ~1500 stocks; ricklefs Hilborn-Branch global meta-analysis.

slides.title: Beyond single species: EBFM + aquaculture + climate
slides.body:
**Ecosystem-based fisheries management (EBFM)**: manage entire ecosystem, not just stocks one-by-one.

Features:
- Account for trophic interactions (predator-prey, competition).
- Habitat conservation.
- Bycatch minimization.
- Spatial management (MPAs).
- Climate adaptation.
- Integrate fishery, biodiversity, climate goals.

**Ecosystem models**:
- **Ecopath with Ecosim (EwE)**: trophic mass-balance; widely used.
- **Atlantis**: end-to-end (physics + biogeochem + food web + fishery + management).
- **OSMOSE**: individual-based.
- **Models of intermediate complexity (MICE)**: 5-10 species focus.
- **Earth-system + DGVM integration** for climate projections.

**Marine protected areas (MPAs)**:
- ~8% of global ocean designated (target: 30% by 2030, '30x30' UN BBNJ Treaty 2023).
- Range: no-take reserves to multi-use.
- Evidence: well-enforced no-take MPAs increase biomass 3-5× (Lester 2009 meta-analysis).
- Spillover benefits to surrounding fisheries.

**Aquaculture**:
- Now > capture in tonnage (since 2014). ~85M tonnes 2021.
- Asia dominates (~90%): China, Indonesia, India, Vietnam.
- Species: salmon, shrimp, tilapia, carp, oyster, mussel, seaweed.
- Pros: predictable supply; lower bycatch; can offset wild-fishery pressure.
- Cons: pollution + waste; disease + parasites (sea lice in salmon); escapes interbreeding with wild; feed (fishmeal/oil from wild — 'fish to feed fish' tension).
- Innovations: recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS); offshore + integrated multi-trophic; insect-meal feeds; selectively bred + sterile triploid stock.

**Climate change + fisheries**:
- **Range shifts**: ~70 km/decade poleward (Pinsky 2013) → trans-boundary issues, e.g., NEAFC mackerel war.
- **Productivity changes**: declining in tropics; mixed in temperate; complex in polar.
- **Phenology mismatches**: zooplankton-fish timing.
- **Acidification**: shell-forming species; pteropods + bivalves.
- **Deoxygenation**: habitat compression for pelagics.
- **Marine heatwaves**: e.g., 'Blob' 2013-16 → ecosystem disruption Pacific NW.

**The next 25 years** will determine whether global fisheries can deliver food security under climate change + biodiversity loss. EBFM + MPAs + climate-adaptive harvest + aquaculture all need to work together.

question.question: Compute MSY + sustainable harvest for a logistic stock
question.goal: Stock has r = 0.4/yr, K = 100k tonnes. Compute B_MSY, MSY, F_MSY, and harvest at B = 60k tonnes.

hints: Maximum of surplus production rB(1-B/K) at B=K/2.
steps.reveal: Surplus production = r B (1-B/K); max at dY/dB = r(1 - 2B/K) = 0 → B_MSY = K/2 = 50k tonnes.
MSY = r B_MSY (1 - B_MSY/K) = 0.4 × 50 × 0.5 = 10k tonnes/yr. Equivalently rK/4 = 0.4 × 100 / 4 = 10k tonnes/yr.

hints: Fishing mortality at MSY = MSY / B_MSY.

steps.reveal: Surplus production at B = 60k: Y = 0.4 × 60 × (1 - 60/100) = 0.4 × 60 × 0.4 = 9.6k tonnes/yr. Slightly less than MSY (10k) because B > B_MSY. Best management: keep B above B_MSY for resilience (precaution + climate uncertainty) → harvest at FMSY/0.8 or similar.

question.question: Why is the MSY paradigm increasingly augmented by precautionary harvest below B_MSY?
options: MSY is mathematically a knife-edge: at B_MSY = K/2, any overshoot risks crashing the stock — there's no margin. Uncertainty in r + K + recruitment + climate make the true B_MSY uncertain. Allee effects + multi-stable states mean recovery is not guaranteed after collapse. Modern reference points use F < F_MSY (e.g., 80% F_MSY) + B > B_MSY (e.g., 1.5 × B_MSY) for safety margin. Pew + UN BBNJ + most modern fishery science adopts this. The Newfoundland cod collapse + Pacific anchoveta crashes + many others vindicated this precaution.
question.explanation: MSY is a knife-edge; precautionary harvest (F < F_MSY, B > B_MSY) gives margin against uncertainty + Allee effects + climate. Newfoundland cod (1992) + Peruvian anchoveta (1972) + others vindicated precaution. Modern stock assessment + harvest control rules embed this.

hints: What's the risk of fishing exactly at MSY?
slides.workedSolution: MSY is a mathematical knife-edge: B_MSY is unstable optimum + small overshoot risks collapse. Precaution (F < F_MSY, B > B_MSY) gives margin against uncertainty (r, K, recruitment, climate) + Allee effects (post-collapse recovery slow/impossible). Foundational to modern stock assessment; vindicated by Newfoundland cod (1992) + Peruvian anchoveta (1972) collapses.

question.question: Drag to typical poleward range shift for marine species (km/decade).
question.explanation: Marine species shift ~70 km/decade poleward (Pinsky 2013; Poloczanska 2013) — about 5× faster than terrestrial species, due to ocean's high heat capacity + connectivity. Drives trans-boundary fishery disputes (e.g., Atlantic mackerel between NE-Atlantic states); food security challenges; ecosystem reorganization.

question.question: Classify each fisheries management tool by its primary mechanism.

items.label: Territorial use rights (TURF, e.g., Chile's loco)

question.explanation: Fisheries management toolkit: catch/effort (TAC, days); spatial (MPA, closures); gear (mesh, bycatch reducers, devices); rights-based (ITQ, TURF, co-management). Modern systems blend multiple tools + adapt over time. Effectiveness depends on enforcement + monitoring + stakeholder buy-in.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why marine protected areas (MPAs) are central to '30 by 30' biodiversity targets.
question.rubric: Mentions: '30x30' (protect 30% of land + ocean by 2030) emerged from CBD + UN BBNJ Treaty 2023. MPAs: well-enforced no-take reserves increase biomass 3-5× (Lester 2009 meta-analysis), spillover benefits to adjacent fisheries, biodiversity preservation, climate-refugia identification, ecosystem-service maintenance (carbon, coastal protection, tourism). Major examples: Papahanaumokuakea (Hawaii), Ross Sea, Chagos, GBR, Phoenix Islands. As of 2024, ~8% of ocean designated; ~3% actually well-protected. Challenges: distant high-seas governance (BBNJ Treaty), enforcement, paper parks, fisher displacement, climate change still affects MPA species. Co-management with local communities + indigenous-led conservation (Hawaii, NZ, Canada, Australia) shown effective. Concludes: MPAs work when well-designed + enforced + locally supported; combined with EBFM + climate mitigation, they anchor the global ocean-biodiversity agenda.
